content: 1. The risk of selected serious adverse events (AEs) associated with voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) is higher in individuals under 15 years of age compared to those older than 15. However, due to potential underreporting, the data does not provide precise risk estimates. More age-specific data is required to better understand these risks. 2. Among all tetanus cases reported to the World Health Organization (WHO) since 2012, only 21% occurred in the 10–14-year age group, despite this group accounting for approximately 46% of VMMC procedures during that time. This highlights the need for booster vaccinations, particularly for adolescent boys, as emphasized in the 2017 WHO tetanus vaccine position paper. 3. Research priorities for ensuring the safety of adolescents undergoing VMMC include collecting surveillance data on moderate, severe, and serious AEs, disaggregated by age and method, and assessing healthcare providers' ability to evaluate adolescents' physical development and capacity for informed consent. 4. Between 2015 and 2019, 41 cases of urethral fistula were reported to PEPFAR, with age-specific data showing varying rates of occurrence. This underscores the importance of monitoring and addressing adverse events in VMMC programs. 5. Programmatic data suggests that VMMC is acceptable among adolescent boys and their parents, with approximately 70% of clients in scale-up programs being adolescents. However, studies on acceptability, particularly differentiating parental and peer influences, are limited. 6. In a Tanzanian study, 95–97% of parents supported VMMC for their sons, with two-thirds of women preferring prepubertal circumcision (12 years or younger) due to faster wound healing, less bleeding, and reduced pain. Other studies have shown that younger adolescents (10–14 years) are primarily motivated by HIV protection, while pain is the main barrier. 7. Trials comparing conventional surgery and device-based methods indicate that younger adolescents heal more quickly. However, keloids have been identified as a potential long-term complication, with genetic predisposition playing a role, particularly among individuals of African descent. 8. Phimosis and adhesions, common in prepubertal males, are contraindications for certain circumcision methods, such as the forceps-guided and some device-based techniques. These conditions may require resolution before proceeding with VMMC. 9. Studies in three countries have shown that phimosis and adhesions are more prevalent among younger adolescents, with ineligibility rates for device-based methods ranging from 40–56% in boys aged 10–13 years. This suggests that VMMC services for younger adolescents may need to be delayed until they are more physically developed. 10. The Tanner stages of development highlight variability in male genital maturity, with most boys aged 10–13 years in Tanner stage 1. This variability necessitates careful consideration of physical development before providing VMMC services to younger adolescents. 11. Modeling studies indicate that the greatest short-term impact on HIV incidence would be achieved by expanding VMMC coverage among men aged 20–34 years, as this group is at the highest risk of HIV infection. However, circumcision of younger adolescents still provides long-term public health benefits, albeit with delayed impact. 12. VMMC services offer additional health benefits, including tetanus toxoid vaccination, HIV testing, safer sex education, and STI management. These services can serve as an entry point for adolescent boys into the healthcare system and contribute to universal health coverage. 13. WHO guidance emphasizes the importance of integrating VMMC with other health interventions, such as deworming, HPV vaccination, and health education, to provide comprehensive care for adolescents. 14. Traditional male circumcision practices, which are common in some communities, may pose public health safety concerns. Poor outcomes from traditional methods highlight the need for safe, medically supervised procedures.
